newsitem.title: FRANCE: French CGT union rail chief warns of showdown.
newsitem.headline: French CGT union rail chief warns of showdown.

text.p: The French government must abandon plans to create a separate rail infrastructure company or else face a showdown with railworkers, Bernard Thibault, head of the Communist-led CGT trade union's rail federation said on Tuesday.

Thibault said planned legislation to create such a company, already put on hold by the government amid union disquiet, should be scrapped in favour of a return to the traditional multi-annual contract between the state and the SNCF railways.

"There are two options. Talks can resume on a different basis to the one decided in October or the transport minister sticks to his guns, says the legislation is the right way and that we have read it wrongly," Thibault said in an interview in daily Les Echos.
"If he picks the latter, we're headed for a showdown."

"We want a multi-annual contract which spells out financial relations between the state and the SNCF in the medium to long term and a strategy over several years," said Thibault, who meets transport minister Bernard Pons on Thursday.

"We have never contested such a contract. It's the content which was contested," he said, referring to the contract which was scrapped by Alain Juppe's centre-right government after a crippling rail strike last November and December.

Following the strikes, the government has opted for a change from the traditional five-year contract with the SNCF in favour of a reform which would involve creating a state holding company to take over at least 125 billion francs of SNCF debt and become owner of the infrastructure.
But the CGT, the biggest union in the SNCF, as well as the CFDT Socialist union, have objected to the latest strategy.

While railworkers' early pension rights are no longer in question -- one of the main reasons for the strike last year -- unions are uneasy about creating a separate infrastructure owner which they believe could be a precursor to privatisation if ever political imperatives changed.
They are also campaigning for greater job security and against deregulation of any kind.

Thibault said things had changed since the 1995 strike but that there was the same problem of "misreading" as last time and unions were already in the "starting blocks" for mobilisation at local and regional level against any move they resented.
"If the case arose, this would make coordination at the national level easier," he said.
Asked if this was likely, he said: "No one can tell. It is not our desire to spearhead more widespread action. We know that we do not want to fall back into that scenario.

"But it is not because of this that we will not find ourselves back at the centre of a much wider movement than that of the railworkers, concerning for example the public-private sector debate. There's no shortage of reasons for such a move."

Bernard Pons, apparently set on calming trade union unease and worries in parliament, said on November 5 that the bill on the reform of the SNCF and the creation of the infrastructure company would be kept on hold pending wider consultations.
"We will open the broadest, clearest and most detailed consultation possible with parliament and unions," he said at the time.
